Clinical Vignette: Amara

Amara sits in the chair across from me with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her shoulders drawn up toward her ears. She is a woman of deliberate composure-it's something she's learned to do well over her thirty years, and especially in the three years since the incident. She works as a school counselor at a large urban middle school, a position she describes as "meaningful, most days," though her voice carries a flatness when she says it now.

Six months ago, Amara was pulled over by police while driving home from work. She was speeding slightly, she acknowledges, distracted by a text message from her husband. The officer approached her window with his hand on his holster. Amara, who is Black and has always been cautious in these interactions, kept her hands visible on the steering wheel. She was polite, compliant, searching his face for any sign of what might happen next. The officer asked for her license and registration. She reached slowly for the glove compartment. In that moment, something shifted in his posture. His hand moved toward his weapon. He shouted at her to keep her hands where he could see them. Her heart seized. Time seemed to fracture. She froze, unable to move, unable to explain that she was simply getting her documents. Another officer arrived. The situation de-escalated. She was given a warning and sent on her way.

But Amara did not go back to her usual self.

Now, when she drives, her hands grip the wheel so tightly her knuckles blanch white. She takes only familiar routes, avoiding highways where she might be more visible to patrol cars. She's been pulled over twice since then-routine traffic stops-and both times she experienced what she describes as her "body shutting down." Her vision narrowed. Her breath became shallow and rapid. She felt as though she were drowning in air. The second time, she couldn't remember what the officer had asked her; she sat in complete dissociation until he returned her license.

At home, her husband has noticed the change. She startles at sudden noises-the doorbell, a car backfiring, even the sound of sirens in the distance sends her into a state of hypervigilance that takes hours to settle. Some nights she doesn't sleep at all, her mind cycling through what-ifs, imagining scenarios where that traffic stop ended differently. She checks the locks on their front door repeatedly before bed, sometimes five or six times, unable to feel confident they're secure.

At work, where she counsels adolescents through their own struggles, Amara finds herself increasingly disconnected. She listens to her students' stories of anxiety and fear, and intellectually she knows how to help them. But she feels hollowed out, going through the motions of empathy she no longer quite feels. During a staff meeting last week, a colleague mentioned a news story about police accountability, and Amara felt a surge of anger so intense it frightened her. She excused herself and sat in her office for twenty minutes, breathing deliberately, trying to regain control of emotions she couldn't quite name.

She describes feeling trapped between two versions of herself-the competent professional who helps young people navigate their trauma, and this newer version, someone she doesn't recognize, someone who is afraid in ways she never was before. The violation of that moment in her car, the helplessness of being perceived as a threat simply for existing in that space, has lodged itself somewhere deep inside her. It plays on repeat in her mind, and she cannot seem to fast-forward past it.
